subsection: 6. De Valera in power, Anglo-Irish relations and from Free State to Republic, 1932–1949

notes.b: The Treaty of December 1921 left the Free State short of full sovereignty (complete independent authority over its own affairs). The Cosgrave governments accepted it but used the Commonwealth to widen the Free State's independence step by step, by agreement with Britain.
points: The Treaty, signed on 6 December 1921, gave the Free State dominion status: a self-governing place in the British Commonwealth, but still tied to the Crown. The Civil War followed between those who accepted it and those who rejected it.

The Treaty's symbols of British authority were the oath of allegiance (a promise of loyalty to the Crown), the Governor-General (the King's representative in Ireland), the Crown itself and British use of three Treaty ports: Berehaven (Bantry Bay), Spike Island (Cork Harbour, Cobh) and Lough Swilly.
The Free State joined the League of Nations in 1923 and registered the Treaty there in 1924, treating it as an international agreement rather than an internal British matter. Britain objected.

The Boundary Commission crisis (the dispute over the border with Northern Ireland) ended with the Tripartite Agreement of December 1925, which released the Free State from its share of the imperial debt, so the border question was set aside.

The Imperial Conference of 1926 produced the Balfour Declaration, which described Britain and the dominions as autonomous communities, equal in status and freely associated. Kevin O'Higgins took a leading part for the Free State.

The Statute of Westminster (December 1931) gave the dominions legislative independence by removing the British Parliament's power to override dominion laws. It was the legal foundation for what de Valera did next.
Cosgrave's government held that independence should come by agreement with Britain, so it left the oath, the Governor-General and the Treaty ports in place.
The Free State also kept paying the land annuities (the repayments tenant farmers owed for land bought under the Land Acts) to the British Exchequer, under arrangements of the 1920s.
notes.tip: In a long essay on Anglo-Irish relations, show Cosgrave's cooperation as the first phase, with dates for Balfour (1926) and Westminster (1931). Examiners reward the point that de Valera later built on this Commonwealth work.

notes.b: De Valera had led the anti-Treaty side in the Civil War, and Fianna Fáil's pledge was to remove the oath and the Treaty's symbols. First he had to win power and then secure it.
points: De Valera left Sinn Féin and founded Fianna Fáil in 1926, so that the anti-Treaty republican cause could be pursued through elections. The party entered the Dáil in 1927.
Cumann na nGaedheal, led by W.T. Cosgrave, had governed from 1922 until 1932, which is why Fianna Fáil's victory in 1932 marked a real change of direction.
In the election of February 1932 Fianna Fáil won 72 seats, short of a majority, and governed with the support of Labour.

De Valera became President of the Executive Council (the head of government, the title used until 1937) on 9 March 1932. He was also Minister for External Affairs, so he personally ran relations with Britain.
He then called a snap election in January 1933. Fianna Fáil won 77 seats, an overall majority, so it no longer depended on Labour and could pass the Treaty-dismantling laws that followed.
notes.tip: Do not confuse the titles: de Valera was President of the Executive Council until 1937 and Taoiseach afterwards. Also keep Fianna Fáil (founded 1926) separate from Sinn Féin.

notes.b: De Valera removed the Treaty's symbols one at a time by legislation, relying on the Statute of Westminster and his own Dáil majority. Learn these steps in date order, because each one builds on the last.
points: In autumn 1932 he removed James McNeill as Governor-General after a public dispute with the government. In November 1932 he appointed Domhnall Ua Buachalla, a Fianna Fáil figure and former TD, and gave him only a minimal role, so the office lost its importance.

The Constitution (Removal of Oath) Act, May 1933, ended the oath of fidelity to the King for members of the Oireachtas (the Irish parliament). This is a different thing from the Treaty's oath of allegiance, which it removed in practice.
The Constitution (Amendment No. 22) Act 1933 ended appeals to the Privy Council, the British body that had been the final court of appeal for Irish cases, so Irish courts now had the last word.
The Seanad (the Senate, the upper house) was abolished in 1936.
Edward VIII abdicated in December 1936, which gave de Valera his chance. On 11 December the Constitution (Amendment No. 27) Act removed the Crown and the Governor-General from the Constitution.

On 12 December 1936 the Executive Authority (External Relations) Act brought back a limited role for the King: he acted for the state only in appointing diplomats and signing international agreements.

Britain took no military action and did not accept that the Free State had left the Commonwealth. The Statute of Westminster supported de Valera's constitutional argument, and Britain did not want a confrontation.
notes.tip: The two December 1936 Acts are easy to confuse: Amendment No. 27 (11 December) removed the Crown, and the External Relations Act (12 December) gave the King back a limited role. In a short paragraph, give each step with its date in the right order and link cause to result.

notes.b: De Valera's decision to stop paying the land annuities (the repayments tenant farmers owed for land bought under the Land Acts) became a trade conflict between the two states. It was only ended by the agreements of 1938.
points: The annuities amounted to about £3 million a year. De Valera withheld them from mid-1932, arguing that they were owed to the Irish state, not to Britain.
Britain held that the arrangements of the 1920s bound Ireland to pay. The two sides read those arrangements differently, and this disagreement was the cause of the war.
From July 1932 Britain imposed special duties (extra import taxes) on Irish cattle, beef, butter and other exports, which hit the Irish farmers who depended on the British market.

The Free State responded with duties on British goods such as coal, cement and iron and steel products, and began a policy of self-sufficiency, meaning producing more of what the country needed rather than importing it.
The Coal–Cattle Pact of 1935 exchanged Irish cattle for British coal and slightly reduced the damage, but it did not end the dispute.
Fianna Fáil argued that the conflict was the price of sovereignty, so in rural constituencies it kept its voters. Cosgrave's party attacked the policy as damaging.
notes.tip: Cause-and-result questions ask why the Economic War began and how it ended. Link the annuities to the war, and the 1938 settlement to its end. Remember the 1935 Coal–Cattle Pact is a partial easing, not the 1938 settlement.

notes.h: The Blueshirts and challenges to the government, 1932–1936
notes.b: The first years of Fianna Fáil rule brought a challenge from the right. It strengthened the government's hand and led to the creation of a new opposition party.
points: The Army Comrades Association (ACA) was founded in February 1932 by pro-Treaty ex-officers to protect Cumann na nGaedheal meetings from disruption by the IRA.

In February 1933 de Valera dismissed Eoin O'Duffy as Garda Commissioner (head of the police). O'Duffy took over the ACA in July 1933, when it adopted a blue shirt and a stiff-armed salute, which is why its members became known as the Blueshirts.

The movement was renamed the National Guard in July 1933. A march on Dublin planned for August 1933 was banned, and the National Guard itself was banned in August 1933, though the movement continued under other names.
In September 1933 Cumann na nGaedheal, the National Centre Party and the Blueshirts merged as Fine Gael, with O'Duffy as its first leader. He resigned in 1934, and Cosgrave was leader by 1935.
Vice-Admiral Henry Somerville, a retired naval officer, was killed by the IRA in March 1936. De Valera banned the IRA in June 1936, which removed the Blueshirt and IRA challenge to the state.
O'Duffy later led an Irish Brigade of about 700 men to fight for Franco in Spain in 1936–37.
notes.tip: Keep the three names apart: the Army Comrades Association was the first name, the Blueshirts the movement, and Fine Gael the party formed in September 1933. Say it was the National Guard that was banned in August 1933, not the whole movement.

notes.h: Bunreacht na hÉireann, 1937: drafting, name and status
notes.b: The new constitution replaced the Free State Constitution of 1922 and gave the state a more Irish and Catholic character. It also avoided the word republic (a state with no monarch as head), which only came into use in 1948–49.
points: De Valera drafted it himself, with John Hearne (legal adviser in the Department of External Affairs) and Maurice Moynihan (Secretary to the Government). Catholic clerical advice was also taken.

It was approved in a plebiscite (a referendum on the Constitution, a vote of the whole electorate) on 1 July 1937, held on the same day as a general election, by about 56 per cent to 44 per cent. It came into force on 29 December 1937.

Article 4 named the state Éire, or in the English language, Ireland. Article 5 declared that Ireland was a sovereign, independent, democratic state, so it claimed full independent authority but did not call itself a republic.
The head of state was a President elected for seven years, and the head of government was the Taoiseach, the new title replacing President of the Executive Council.
notes.tip: Do not mix up the Free State Constitution (1922) with Bunreacht na hÉireann (1937), or Éire (the name chosen in 1937) with Republic of Ireland (the description used from 1949). Document questions ask what the 1937 constitution contained.

notes.h: Bunreacht na hÉireann, 1937: territory, family, Church and reactions
notes.b: Three articles show the constitution's character most clearly, and each drew criticism. They claimed the whole island, defined the family in a conservative way and recognised the Catholic Church's special position.
points: Articles 2 and 3 claimed the whole island of Ireland as the national territory, while limiting the exercise of the state's laws to 26 counties until reunification. This was a claim on Northern Ireland without any power there.
Article 41 recognised the family as the foundation of society, spoke of the woman's life within the home, and the Constitution barred divorce.

Article 44 recognised the special position of the Catholic Church as guardian of the faith of the great majority. It also named the Church of Ireland, Presbyterian, Methodist and other churches and the Jewish congregations. The clause was removed in 1972.
Unionists, women's groups and some nationalists criticised the document.
Douglas Hyde was inaugurated as the first President on 25 June 1938.
notes.tip: Constitution questions ask what Articles 2–3, 41 and 44 said and why critics objected. Score by stating what the article said and giving one reaction, not by quoting the article number alone.

notes.b: Three agreements signed in London on 25 April 1938 settled the main disputes between the two governments. They also removed the Treaty's last military restriction, the British hold on the ports.
points: The defence agreement handed over the Treaty ports at Berehaven, Spike Island (Cobh) and Lough Swilly to Ireland, and the handover took place in July 1938.

The financial agreement settled all annuities and other financial claims for a single payment of £10 million, far less than Britain had claimed. This ended the annuities dispute that had caused the Economic War.
The trade agreement ended the special duties on both sides, which brought the Economic War to a close.

Neville Chamberlain, the British Prime Minister, agreed partly to improve relations as war approached, so Britain preferred a friendlier Ireland to a quarrel over the ports. Winston Churchill opposed giving up the ports.
De Valera raised partition in the talks and linked it to the ports, but Britain would not move on the border.
Controlling its own harbours made it possible for Ireland to remain neutral in 1939.
notes.tip: Cause-and-result questions ask why Britain gave up the ports in 1938: give Chamberlain's wish for better relations as war approached and mention Churchill's opposition. Do not confuse these 1938 Agreements (ports, annuities, trade) with the 1935 Coal–Cattle Pact.

notes.b: The inter-party government formally ended the External Relations Act and left the Commonwealth. Britain responded by guaranteeing Northern Ireland's position.
points: Fianna Fáil lost its majority in the general election of 4 February 1948. John A. Costello of Fine Gael became Taoiseach on 18 February 1948 at the head of an inter-party government (Fine Gael, Labour, Clann na Poblachta, Clann na Talmhan and others).

Seán MacBride, leader of Clann na Poblachta, was Minister for External Affairs. He wanted to repeal the External Relations Act, which he regarded as an anomaly because it still gave the King a role in Irish diplomacy.
Costello announced the decision in Ottawa in September 1948. The causes of the announcement are disputed.
The Republic of Ireland Act was passed in December 1948 and came into force on Easter Monday, 18 April 1949. It repealed the External Relations Act and ended the state's link with the Commonwealth.
The British Ireland Act 1949 recognised that Ireland was no longer a member of the Commonwealth, but said Irish citizens would not be treated as foreigners.
It also declared that Northern Ireland would remain in the United Kingdom unless the Parliament of Northern Ireland consented to change, which strengthened the unionist position.
The southern parties united in an anti-partition campaign in 1949, but it achieved little.
Independence had largely been achieved by 1938, so 1949 was the formal break with the Crown and the Commonwealth, not the moment Ireland became independent.
notes.tip: Expect questions on why the Republic was declared in 1948 and what the British replied. Keep apart the Republic of Ireland Act (1948, Irish) and the Ireland Act (1949, British), and Costello (Taoiseach) and MacBride (Minister for External Affairs).

notes.h: Key personality: Éamon de Valera (part 2 and overall evaluation)
notes.b: De Valera dominated the 1930s and 1940s and shaped the state's constitution, relations with Britain and neutrality. He led Fianna Fáil in government from 1932 to 1948, again in 1951–54 and 1957–59, was President of Ireland from 1959 to 1973, and died in 1975. Judgements about him are divided.
points: Between 1932 and 1948 he removed the oath, the Governor-General and the Privy Council appeal, passed the 1936 Acts, drafted the 1937 constitution, secured the ports in 1938, banned the IRA in 1936 and kept Ireland neutral in the Second World War.

Events shaped him as well. The Statute of Westminster gave him room to act, the abdication gave him his chance in 1936, the Blueshirts strengthened his hand against opponents, and the approach of war helped persuade Britain to give up the ports.
He was a direct participant: as his own Minister for External Affairs he negotiated personally with Britain, and he drafted the 1937 constitution himself with Hearne and Moynihan.
He did not end partition, and the Economic War cost the farming economy dearly.
The social and economic record was weak, with high emigration and unemployment, a conservative Catholic constitution and wartime censorship.

Contemporaries: supporters, especially small farmers and workers, saw him as the man who finished the work of independence. Opponents in Cumann na nGaedheal and the Blueshirts called him a dictator, or said he damaged the economy for the sake of symbols.

Historians: J.J. Lee (Ireland 1912–1985, 1989) credits him with consolidating democracy and with strong political skills, while criticising the economy. Deirdre McMahon (Republicans and Imperialists, 1984) examined his diplomacy with Britain.
Tim Pat Coogan (De Valera: Long Fellow, Long Shadow, 1993) is critical, while Diarmaid Ferriter (Judging Dev, 2007) is balanced, stressing both his stubbornness and his pragmatism.
notes.tip: For an overall assessment, give successes (symbols removed, ports, constitution, neutrality) and failures (partition, Economic War, social and economic record). Credit goes for weighing the short term against the long term and for naming a historian with a view.

notes.h: Assessment: Cosgrave or de Valera in Anglo-Irish relations
notes.b: Both leaders increased Irish independence, but by different methods and at different costs. Weigh them in pairs: what each achieved, and what each left undone.
points: Cosgrave's strengths: he secured the Free State's international recognition, used the Commonwealth to widen independence, and avoided economic conflict with Britain.
Cosgrave's limits: he left the oath, the Governor-General and the ports in place, and the Boundary Commission failed.

De Valera's strengths: he removed the symbols of the Treaty, settled the ports and the annuities, and created a constitution that Britain accepted in practice. His ports settlement also made neutrality possible.
De Valera's limits: the Economic War, the failure to end partition, and the fact that his changes relied on the groundwork Cosgrave laid at the Imperial Conferences (Balfour and Westminster).
Contemporary view: Fianna Fáil supporters said de Valera achieved real sovereignty, while Fine Gael said he damaged the economy for the sake of symbols.
Later view: the Republic of 1949 is often judged mainly a formal act, because de Valera had already made independence real. Neither leader ended partition.
notes.tip: In a Cosgrave or de Valera comparison, give a clear verdict at the start, then paired strengths and limits for each. Make the point that de Valera built on Cosgrave's Commonwealth work, and say what each achieved, not only what each wanted.

keyTerms.definition: Full independent authority over the state's affairs, the aim of de Valera's constitutional changes of the 1930s.
A state without a monarch as head; Ireland was declared a republic by the Republic of Ireland Act, in force on 18 April 1949.
The Free State's Treaty status within the Commonwealth, which de Valera gradually dismantled.
The loyalty to the Crown expressed in the Treaty oath, which was removed in 1933.
The 1931 British Act giving dominions legislative independence, which de Valera used to change the Treaty.
The 1933 Act ending the oath for members of the Oireachtas.
The 1936 Act that gave the King a role only in diplomatic appointments and treaties; repealed in 1948–49.
The 1932–38 trade dispute between Britain and Ireland over the land annuities.
The repayments tenant farmers made for land purchased under the Land Acts, collected by the Irish state and paid to Britain.
The Army Comrades Association, later the National Guard, led by Eoin O'Duffy and banned in 1933.
The constitution of 1937, which replaced the Free State Constitution.
The 1948 Act, in force from 18 April 1949, that declared the state a republic and left the Commonwealth.
